title: Physiological functions in plants
blurb: Plant physiology: its 5 key areas and what it studies.
lede: Plant physiology: its 5 key areas and what it studies. Phytochemistry and secondary metabolites; cell signalling and cell–cell communication (plasmodesmata, symplast vs apoplast); growth and development terms (totipotency, differentiation, dedifferentiation). Plant tissues (meristem; parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) and organs (leaf, flower, root, stem; taproot vs fibrous root). Mineral nutrition (Liebig's law of the minimum; 17 essential elements; macro- and micronutrients with uptake forms and roles). Symbioses: mycorrhizae (ecto-, arbuscular, orchid, ericoid, arbutoid, monotropoid), root-nodule bacteria (Rhizobium), parasitic plants (haustoria). Transport: xylem vs phloem, transpiration stream, stomata and guard cells, translocation. Biomechanics and environmental physiology; C3/C4/CAM recap. Pigments (chlorophylls, carotenoids, anthocyanins, betalains). Phytohormones (auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins, ABA, ethylene, brassinosteroids, jasmonates, salicylic acid, strigolactones). Plant movements (tropisms, nastic movements), photoperiodism (phytochrome Pr/Pfr, cryptochrome), circadian rhythms, and model plant organisms.

Mycorrhiza types (ECM: Hartig net; AM: arbuscules; orchid, ericoid)

cards.lede: Read the question, answer it out loud, then flip the card.

items.n: Five key areas of plant physiology?
items.a: Phytochemistry, cellular interactions, molecular & cell biology, plant morphology, environmental interactions.

items.n: What are plasmodesmata?
items.a: Channels connecting the cytosol of neighbouring plant cells (symplastic transport); pass molecules < 1,000 Da, regulated up to 10,000 Da.

items.n: Symplastic vs apoplastic transport?
items.a: Symplastic: through cytoplasm via plasmodesmata. Apoplastic: through cell walls between microfibrils (water, minerals).

items.n: What is totipotency?
items.a: The ability of a plant cell to regenerate a whole plant under appropriate conditions.

items.n: Three permanent plant tissues?
items.a: Parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma.

items.n: Which tissue is dead with lignified walls?
items.a: Sclerenchyma (rigidity, strength).

items.n: Which tissue has walls thickened at the corners and gives flexibility?
items.a: Collenchyma.

items.n: What are chlorenchyma and aerenchyma?
items.a: Photosynthetic parenchyma / parenchyma with large air spaces (buoyancy in aquatic plants).

items.n: Parts of the stamen and of the pistil?
items.a: Stamen: filament + anther. Pistil: stigma + style + ovary.

items.n: Taproots vs fibrous roots occur in?
items.a: Taproots in dicots and gymnosperms; fibrous roots in monocots and most grasses.

items.n: State Liebig's law of the minimum.
items.a: Without an essential nutrient the plant cannot complete its life cycle; growth is limited by the scarcest nutrient.

items.n: How many essential plant elements are there?
List the macronutrients.
items.a: N, P, K, Ca, S, Mg (+ C, O, H).

items.n: List the micronutrients.
items.a: Fe, B, Cl, Mn, Zn, Cu, Mo, Ni.

items.n: Which element is essential for chlorophyll?
items.a: Magnesium (Mg²⁺).

items.n: In which forms is nitrogen taken up?
items.a: NO₃⁻ and NH₄⁺.

items.n: Role of boron?
items.a: Cross-linking pectin.

items.n: How old is plant–mycorrhizal symbiosis?
items.a: About 475 million years.

items.n: What is the Hartig net?
items.a: Fungal hyphae growing between root cortex cells in ectomycorrhizae.

items.n: Benefits of ectomycorrhiza to trees?
items.a: More nutrients (especially P), larger soil volume, more active root area, tolerance to drought/heat/pH/heavy metals, protection against pathogens.

items.n: What does the fungus get from the plant?
items.a: 4–20 % of the plant's photosynthetically fixed carbon.

items.n: Most common mycorrhiza type and its fungal group?
items.a: Arbuscular mycorrhiza (~72 %), Glomeromycota.

items.n: What are arbuscules?
items.a: Tree-like branched hyphae inside root cells in AM; they break down after ~2 weeks, releasing nutrients.

items.n: Why do orchids need mycorrhiza at germination?
items.a: Their tiny seeds lack reserves; the fungus supplies carbohydrates.

items.n: Which plants have ericoid mycorrhiza?
items.a: Ericaceae (heather, blueberries, cranberries, Rhododendron) on acidic, poor soils; fungus Hymenoscyphus ericae.

items.n: Which bacteria form root nodules, and with which family?
items.a: Rhizobium, Bradyrhizobium; with Fabaceae (legumes).

items.n: What are haustoria?
items.a: Modified roots of parasitic plants that connect to the host's vascular bundles (e.g. mistletoe, Cuscuta).

items.n: What does xylem carry, and in which direction?
items.a: Water and minerals, upward only (unidirectional); dead tissue.

items.n: What does phloem carry, and in which direction?
items.a: Sugars (sucrose) and amino acids, both ways from source to sink; living tissue.

items.n: Two types of xylem conducting cells?
items.a: Vessels (long, multicellular, no end walls) and tracheids (single, shorter, dead).

items.n: What is the transpiration pull?
items.a: Suction created by water evaporating from leaves that draws water up from the roots.

items.n: How do guard cells open a stoma?
items.a: By day they accumulate sugar, take in water by osmosis, become turgid and bend apart.

items.n: What is translocation?
items.a: Active (ATP-using) transport of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem.

items.n: When and why did C4 plants evolve?
items.a: When CO₂ fell in the Miocene, making photorespiration very limiting.

items.n: Another name for the C4 pathway?
items.a: Hatch–Slack cycle.

items.n: Which pigments are porphyrins absorbing red and blue light?
items.a: Chlorophylls.

items.n: Which algae have chlorophyll c instead of b?
items.a: Kelps, diatoms and other heterokonts.

items.n: Name three carotenoids and their colours.
items.a: Carotene (orange), lutein (yellow), lycopene (red, tomatoes).

items.n: How do betalains differ from anthocyanins?
items.a: Betalains come from tyrosine, occur only in Caryophyllales (e.g. beetroot) and never co-occur with anthocyanins.

items.n: Why do plants not need hormone glands?
items.a: Every plant cell can produce hormones.

items.n: Six main classes of phytohormones?
items.a: Auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins, abscisic acid, ethylene, brassinosteroids.

items.n: Main auxin, and who isolated it?
items.a: Indole-3-acetic acid (IAA); Kögl, 1933, from human urine.

items.n: Main functions of auxins?
items.a: Cell enlargement, bud formation, root initiation, tropisms.

items.n: Main functions of cytokinins?
items.a: Cell division, shoot formation, delaying senescence.

items.n: From which organism were gibberellins first isolated?
items.a: The fungus Gibberella fujikuroi (abnormal rice growth).

items.n: What do gibberellins promote?
items.a: Cell elongation.

items.n: Roles of abscisic acid?
items.a: Growth inhibitor; dormancy, seed drying, leaf fall; closes stomata under water stress.

items.n: Which hormone is a gas, and what does it do?
items.a: Ethylene: fruit ripening; stops elongation and makes stems thicken.

items.n: Only steroid hormones in plants?
items.a: Brassinosteroids (brassinolide, rapeseed pollen, 1979).

items.n: Jasmonates vs salicylic acid in defence?
items.a: Jasmonates: against herbivores and necrotrophic pathogens. Salicylic acid: against biotrophic pathogens.

items.n: What do strigolactones do?
items.a: Promote AM fungi and parasitic weed germination (Striga); inhibit shoot branching.

items.n: Three steps of a tropism?
items.a: Perception, signal transduction, directional growth.

items.n: Root vs shoot gravitropism?
items.a: Roots positive (toward gravity); shoots negative (against gravity).

items.n: Tropism vs nastic movement?
items.a: Tropism: directional growth set by stimulus direction, slow. Nastic: independent of stimulus direction, faster, growth or turgor.

items.n: What is thigmonasty?
items.a: A nastic response to touch.

items.n: What is photoperiodism?
items.a: A plant's response to the length of the night/dark period (e.g. flowering).

items.n: Three photoperiodic groups of plants?
items.a: Short-day, long-day, day-neutral.

items.n: How does red vs far-red light affect phytochrome?
items.a: Red converts Pr → Pfr (active); far-red converts Pfr → Pr (inactive).

items.n: Which light do cryptochromes absorb?
items.a: Blue light and UV-A.

items.n: Which gene cluster controls cyanobacterial circadian rhythm?
items.a: kaiABC (Synechococcus).

items.n: Which plant has the smallest genome?
items.a: Selaginella moellendorffii (a lycophyte).
